before: Use an empty parent folder, Python 3.12, and the chapter 1 bootstrap commands. Generate project_manager yourself and activate the generated project environment.

scenes.say: By the end, a signed-in user can create projects, manage tasks, and see progress. Staff have a separate Admin, and help content comes from the CMS. We will build the backend first, then connect the browser to APIs we have already tested.
scenes.type: The README clone, virtual-environment and dependency commands. Explain which activation command belongs to Windows and which to macOS/Linux.
scenes.show: Preview registration, one project, a completed task, and the Help page. Show staff Admin briefly without exposing passwords.

scenes.say: Flaxon owns the Python server. Teloce compiles our HTML components into JavaScript. MinifyJS optimizes the compiled JavaScript for production; we do not need a Node build for this project.
scenes.type: In a separate folder: flaxon new project-manager --no-venv, then cd project-manager and python management.py migrate.
scenes.show: Run flaxon welcome and flaxon welcome-status. Open the generated welcome page and show its module folder.

scenes.say: The starter is our beginning, and the completed repository is our reference. The course uses pinned dependencies, including an explicitly labelled Flaxon build with CMS fixes.
scenes.type: Create prepare_course.py exactly as printed in this chapter, run it, and install the copied pinned dependencies. Do not copy finished application code. The CSS adaptation happens in chapter 8.
scenes.show: Point to the generated welcome module, flaxon_cli.py, management.py, and ui/app.html. The raw starter still has its generated stylesheet until chapter 8.

cut: Cut package download waits, not the commands or their successful completion. Record a clean ten-second microphone test before this take.
finish: State that the welcome project runs, then introduce modules as the next step.

before: Open the generated starter and keep the final app.py available in a separate reference window. Do not mount a feature before its imports and module exist.

scenes.say: A feature can keep its Python routes, browser screens, and commands together. The application factory decides which features are mounted and where their APIs begin.
scenes.type: create_app() and the welcome module mount in app.py. Introduce settings.py and the module directory structure.
scenes.show: Trace GET /api/welcome/status from the application mount to the module decorator.

scenes.say: A prefix is added once. A slash inside a project module will become /api/projects/ when we mount that module. Tests can create a fresh app against a temporary database.
scenes.type: The FlaxonModule declaration in modules/projects/module.py as a preview; save its UI mapping for the frontend chapter.
scenes.show: Contrast a Python route parameter with a browser :id pattern. Show the module-owned files rather than inventing a new routing API.

cut: Keep the architecture explanation short. Zoom in on one mount and one route; do not tour every framework file.
finish: Ask the learner to find the welcome API and its module command.

before: Open the generated teaching project and the chapter file blocks. Select DATA_DIR=data/course_recording before applying the course migration. Leave any starter database alone.

scenes.say: A user owns projects, and each project owns tasks. We store those relationships in the database, so they survive a server restart.
scenes.type: The users, projects, and tasks definitions in the migration; then the session and auth-attempt tables. Explain foreign keys, cascades, and indexes.
scenes.show: Run migrate and migrate --status. Run migrate again and show that no duplicate migration is applied.

scenes.say: SQLite calls are synchronous. Our small repository runs them in a worker thread and opens a connection for each operation. Values use placeholders rather than being joined into SQL.
scenes.type: Database.connection(), all(), one(), and execute() in that order.
scenes.show: Point to PRAGMA foreign_keys and the transaction context. Show that the database path comes from DATA_DIR, not a hardcoded cloud path.

cut: Print or enlarge the migration SQL when explaining relationships; the JSON string is difficult to read at normal editor size.
finish: Recap persistence, parameterized values, and why migrations precede API writes.

before: The schema and Database helper must run. Use chapter-04-auth as a recovery point; customer UI and staff Admin are deliberately not enabled in that checkpoint.

scenes.say: We never store a plain password. Argon2 hashes the password, while a random opaque session token identifies an authenticated session. Only a digest of that token is stored.
scenes.type: security.py: digest(), read_session(), require_user(), and session_response(); then the auth module register and login handlers.
scenes.show: Show GET /api/auth/session before login, the registration response, and the public user fields without printing password hashes.

scenes.say: Cookies alone are not enough for these mutations. A session-bound CSRF token is required, and login rotates both the session and that token.
scenes.type: check_csrf(), then the logout handler. Explain HttpOnly, SameSite, production Secure, and expiry while pointing to the actual code.
scenes.show: In the HTTP client, deliberately use the old CSRF token after registration and show rejection; then use the new token successfully.

scenes.say: Logging out must revoke the old server session. A cookie copied before logout should stop working too.
scenes.type: The logout/revocation test in the auth checkpoint, or explain the completed login/logout test.
scenes.show: Run authentication tests and show a wrong-password response. Never use a staff credential in the public registration example.

cut: Pause after session rotation. This is a concept learners need to reproduce, not a place to speed up typing.
finish: Ask viewers to replay an old cookie after logout and predict the status.

before: Start from the authenticated backend. Open the project module, the HTTP demonstration, and the ownership test. Use two separate learner accounts.

scenes.say: The owner comes from the signed-in user. It is not a field the browser gets to choose.
scenes.type: owned_project(), list_projects(), and create_project(), including imports, validation, SQL placeholders, and the 201 response.
scenes.show: Create a project through HTTP, list it, and show the consistent data envelope.

scenes.say: Authentication tells us who you are. Ownership tells us which record you may use. A private record returns 404 to someone else.
scenes.type: get_project(), update_project(), and delete_project(). Explain the CSRF and ownership checks before mutations.
scenes.show: Run scripts/course_api_demo.py, then the ownership test. Show a blank name returning 400 and another account getting 404.

cut: This is the backend half of the pilot. Keep one successful request and one denied request visible long enough to read.
finish: Transition to tasks: tasks will inherit permission through their parent project.

before: Project creation and ownership must be working. Prepare one owned project and a second account.

scenes.say: A task belongs to a project. Every operation checks that the current user may access the parent project, even when the request only contains a task ID.
scenes.type: owned_task(), list_tasks(), and create_task() in modules/tasks/module.py.
scenes.show: Create a task with a due date and demonstrate that another user cannot add a task to your project.

scenes.say: PATCH changes only supplied fields. Status is one of three values, and a date uses YYYY-MM-DD. These rules belong on the server as well as the form.
scenes.type: task_fields(), update_task(), and delete_task(); type the optional list status filter.
scenes.show: Update a task to done, filter to done, reject an impossible date, and show the cascade test for project deletion.

cut: Do not spend the take typing repetitive SQL punctuation silently. Explain the changed values and ownership decision.
finish: Ask the learner to add an invalid-date regression case.

before: Keep the API layer working before showing any customer interface code. Use disposable tests, never the recording database.

scenes.say: These tests make requests through the ASGI application. A temporary database gives each test an isolated place to create records.
scenes.type: The application fixture and Account helper in tests/conftest.py. Explain how the helper carries the cookie and CSRF token.
scenes.show: Show the migration fixture and create_app() receiving temporary paths.

scenes.say: The ownership test registers a second user and calls the API directly. Hiding an Edit button would not pass this test if the backend were wrong.
scenes.type: test_project_crud_and_ownership(), then one invalid task case.
scenes.show: Run focused tests first, then the suite appropriate to your current teaching checkout. The completed reference has additional Admin/CMS tests taught later.

cut: Show failures intentionally only in a throwaway rehearsal checkout; restore the code and end the take with passing checks.
finish: Point to backend-ready and explain that the frontend will consume these same endpoints.

before: The backend must already work. Open ui/app.html, ui/pages/Home.html, app.py, and the module UI route declarations.

scenes.say: Our HTML component has a template, a TypeScript script, and a scoped style block. Flaxon serves the compiled shell; Teloce mounts pages inside the router view.
scenes.type: The shell template and script, app.use_teloce(), and the explicit Python shell routes.
scenes.show: Open the compiled page and trace the router-view marker and module UI mapping.

scenes.say: We keep page styles inside the page. The compiler adds a component scope attribute so a header or button rule does not unexpectedly change another component.
scenes.type: Type the shell style scoped block and Home styles exactly as printed. Explain the deliberate body margin reset. Delete public/app.css at the end of this chapter.
scenes.show: Change the Home button colour, navigate away, and confirm another component's button is unchanged. Restore the final colour.

scenes.say: A parent owns its layout, and a child owns its form. Inherited font and colour can flow through the shell, but scoped selector rules do not become a global stylesheet.
scenes.type: Show the temporary Login, ProjectList, and ProjectDetails placeholders from this chapter; their real forms and local controls are added in chapters 9-10.
scenes.show: Confirm there is no /assets/app.css request. At mobile width, show that the shell navigation wraps and the forms fit.

cut: Teach a few meaningful CSS rules live, then supply the rest of each scoped block in that component. Do not paste one giant global CSS file.
finish: Ask viewers to explain the difference between inheritance and scoped selector matching.

before: The auth API and SPA shell must run. Keep ui/types.ts, ui/api.ts, and Login.html open.

scenes.say: The interface knows the shape of a Session, but the server still validates the real request. Our helper loads the session, sends cookies and CSRF, and unwraps data.
scenes.type: User and Session interfaces, loadSession(), then api(). Explain response.ok and token replacement on auth responses.
scenes.show: Show one successful response and one error without exposing a real session cookie on camera.

scenes.say: The account form tracks loading and errors, disables repeated submissions, and clears the password after success. Switching modes keeps the form DOM with v-show.
scenes.type: Login.html template, data(), mounted(), submit(), logout(), and its scoped form styles.
scenes.show: Register in the browser, sign out, try a wrong password, then sign in. Show the status/alert messages and the keyboard labels.

cut: Slow down when the helper cache changes after authentication. An old CSRF token is a common error worth explaining.
finish: Have learners add explanatory form text without weakening backend validation.

before: An authenticated learner can create a project. Open the detail page, TaskForm.html, and TaskList.html.

scenes.say: The form emits an event; the parent decides how to save it. We keep requests in the page so the child components stay easy to understand.
scenes.type: TaskForm and TaskList templates, props and emits, then the parent createTask(), changeStatus(), and removeTask() methods.
scenes.show: Create a task, change its status, and delete it. Show the child's scoped .card and button rules.

scenes.say: The task signal holds the complete collection. Computed progress reads that signal. The filtered list changes what we show, not the total we use for completion.
scenes.type: signal([]), computed completion, setTasks(), and the mounted effect in ProjectDetails. Do not add signal imports to this compiled HTML component.
scenes.show: Create two tasks and complete one: progress is 50%. Filter to done and confirm it stays 50%.

scenes.say: An effect is work that belongs to the mounted screen. Stop it before unmount so an old screen does not keep reacting.
scenes.type: beforeUnmount() and the mutation busy/error guard; type the local progress style.
scenes.show: Navigate away and back, then check an empty project at 0%. Run the task API tests; the complete browser regression script is introduced in chapter 14.

cut: Explain signal reads with parentheses and writes with .set(). Do not imply ordinary TypeScript helper files receive the compiler's automatic imports.
finish: Ask learners to compute a remaining-task count from the full collection.

before: At least one project and its detail screen must be working. Keep browser Network and a separate console ready.

scenes.say: data-teloce-link tells the browser router to handle an internal anchor. The page mounts in the shell rather than reloading the document.
scenes.type: Internal anchors in app.html and ProjectList.html; show the module's /projects/:id mapping and the id prop.
scenes.show: Set window.courseNavigationMarker = 42, click a project, and read the marker again. Back and Forward should preserve the document.

scenes.say: A refresh starts at the server. Flaxon must return the shell for the browser URL before Teloce can mount the component and fetch its data.
scenes.type: The explicit /projects/<int:project_id> shell route, then the Help shell routes. Explain why Admin links are ordinary anchors.
scenes.show: Refresh a nested project URL and request an unknown /api path to show that API 404 responses are preserved.

cut: Do not hide the refresh check; it is the difference between click-only routing and a usable SPA deployment.
finish: Ask learners to add a Help link and verify click, Back, and refresh.

before: Customer APIs work. Open backoffice.py and management.py. Use only disposable staff credentials during the recording.

scenes.say: Customers and staff are separate account systems. Registering a customer never creates an administrator. We bootstrap staff interactively, with no default password.
scenes.type: AdminDashboard configuration with strict_permissions, then the setup-admin command.
scenes.show: Run setup-admin with the password entry off-screen. Sign into /admin/login and show the model list.

scenes.say: The Admin adapter reuses the same database as the customer API. Staff capabilities decide who can read or change all registered records; this is not a customer tenant portal.
scenes.type: ProjectAdmin get_instances(), get_instance(), update_instance(), and registration fields. Explain why create is disabled here.
scenes.show: Edit a project as authorized staff and read it through its owner account. Create a read-only staff role and show that changes are denied.

cut: Hide passwords and sensitive account data. Show exact permission keys from docs/security.md rather than implying a role name grants everything.
finish: Recap the account boundary and introduce editorial permissions.

before: Staff Admin runs with the patched course build. Open the help content type, public content module, Help.html, and Article/[slug].html.

scenes.say: The CMS stores editorial records. Public readers receive only published articles and a small whitelist of fields; they never use the staff editing API.
scenes.type: The help_article ContentType, published_articles(), the list endpoint, and the slug endpoint.
scenes.show: Create a draft and show that it is absent from the Help page. Publish with a permitted account and load it in the SPA.

scenes.say: Rendering HTML is different from displaying a string. This field is sanitized rich text; we do not render arbitrary user input as HTML.
scenes.type: Help and Article templates, v-html on the sanitized body, and each page's scoped styles.
scenes.show: Show the rendered article and the browser-safe body. Explain that injected HTML does not automatically receive component scope attributes.

scenes.say: Draft editors and publishers have different rights. Editing already published content or restoring a protected revision also needs the required publication permissions.
scenes.type: Show the CMS security patch notes and one permission regression test; do not rewrite the entire framework patch during the lesson.
scenes.show: Demonstrate that a draft-only editor cannot publish. The automated CMS security suite is added and run in chapter 14.

cut: If demonstrating seed, run it only after creating a customer account and restart the process. Do not seed production on every deployment.
finish: Ask learners to prove that a draft is not exposed publicly.

before: The completed app and Playwright Chromium must be installed. Rehearse the browser script before recording its terminal output.

scenes.say: API tests cannot prove that a real form listener, SPA link, or mobile layout works. Our browser checks use fresh data and exercise the actual compiled interface.
scenes.type: Explain the server setup and desktop/mobile loop in scripts/browser_smoke.py; add one behavioral assertion as a teaching example.
scenes.show: Run API checks and the development browser smoke test. Show the scoped form controls and a 390-pixel viewport.

scenes.say: We also test the production build, because minified code should preserve the same behavior. Accessibility is part of the working interface, not a final decoration.
scenes.type: Point to the production switch, status/alert roles, form labels, focus-visible styles, and busy guards.
scenes.show: Run the production browser smoke test. Complete a short keyboard-only workflow and show a visible focus ring.

cut: Cut repetitive automated interactions if they are too fast to teach; keep the purpose, command, and passing result.
finish: List the checks that must pass before the deployment take.

before: Keep the local production tests green. A real deployment take requires your own Render service access; do not say deployment succeeded until you verify it there.

scenes.say: The compiled interface uses MinifyJS. Component CSS is bundled from style scoped blocks; there is no separate app.css file to copy to a server.
scenes.type: Explain scripts/build_ui.py and the build command in render.yaml.
scenes.show: Run the production build and show the component count and browser verification result.

scenes.say: SQLite needs a persistent disk. This course uses one instance and one worker, with both application and Admin databases under /var/data.
scenes.type: Render disk, DATA_DIR, runtime migration/start command, PUBLIC_ORIGIN, DEBUG, and generated secret settings.
scenes.show: In your Render account, configure the actual HTTPS origin and bootstrap staff with the Shell. Keep secrets off-camera.

scenes.say: A successful service screen is not enough. We need a real workflow, denied requests, and data that survives a restart.
scenes.type: Use the verification list in docs/render.md and write down a backup/restore procedure for both SQLite files.
scenes.show: Create a project/task, publish help, refresh a nested route, sign out, confirm API denial, restart, and verify persistence. If you have not deployed, explicitly present this as preparation.

cut: Record the cloud verification after it actually works; do not splice a local test into a claim of live HTTPS verification.
finish: End with the completed application, source/checkpoint links, and one extension exercise. Thank viewers in your own voice.
